claim: Ribbon-type synapses transmit high-bandwidth sensory signals into their postsynaptic networks.
source: Ribbon-type synapses feed high-bandwidth sensory signals into their postsynaptic networks (reviewed in, e.g. Moser et al., 2020; Sterling and Matthews, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles by Moser et al., 2020 and Sterling and Matthews, 2005

claim: Auditory systems typically operate at higher frequencies than visual systems.
source: For example, auditory systems typically operate at higher frequencies than visual systems, and accordingly auditory inner hair cells tend to use 'faster' ribbon synapses compared to those of photoreceptors (Baden et al., 2013a; Moser et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baden et al., 2013a and Moser et al., 2020

claim: Auditory inner hair cells use 'faster' ribbon synapses compared to those of photoreceptors.
source: For example, auditory systems typically operate at higher frequencies than visual systems, and accordingly auditory inner hair cells tend to use 'faster' ribbon synapses compared to those of photoreceptors (Baden et al., 2013a; Moser et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baden et al., 2013a and Moser et al., 2020

claim: Rods and cones differ greatly in the way they use their ribbons.
source: Moreover, amongst photoreceptors of the vertebrate eye, rods and cones tend to differ greatly in the way they use their ribbons (Regus-Leidig and Brandstätter, 2012; Sterling and Matthews, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Regus-Leidig and Brandstätter, 2012 and Sterling and Matthews, 2005

claim: Rods generally have large ribbons that can dock many hundreds of vesicles at a time, concentrated at a single release site.
source: Rods generally have large ribbons that can dock many hundreds of vesicles at a time, concentrated at a single release site, to support focussed, low-noise transmission (e.g. Hays et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hays et al., 2021

claim: Cones usually use multiple smaller ribbons, often positioned at different release sites in a single pedicle.
source: In contrast, cones usually use multiple smaller ribbons, often positioned at different release sites in a single pedicle, to serve diverse postsynaptic circuits (e.g. DeVries et al., 2006; Jackman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeVries et al., 2006 and Jackman et al., 2009

claim: Sharks achieve high-amplitude pulsatile transmission required for predation by combining greatly elongated ribbons with an ion-channel composition that supports broad spiking.
source: For example, sharks achieve high-amplitude pulsatile transmission required for predation by combining greatly elongated ribbons with an ion-channel composition that supports broad spiking.
evidence: This statement is part of a discussion about ribbon synapses in electrosensory organs of elasmobranchs, which is supported by citation to Bellono et al., 2018 in the preceding sentence

claim: Skates drive their smaller ribbons using graded voltage signals to support low-amplitude, oscillatory transmission suitable for intraspecific communication.
source: In contrast, skates drive their smaller ribbons using graded voltage signals to support low-amplitude, oscillatory transmission suitable for intraspecific communication.
evidence: This statement is part of a discussion about ribbon synapses in electrosensory organs of elasmobranchs, which is supported by citation to Bellono et al., 2018 in the preceding sentence

claim: Ribbons and their associated molecular machinery are important structural tuning sites of synaptic function in many sensory systems.
source: This suggests that ribbons and their associated molecular machinery are important structural tuning sites of synaptic function in many sensory systems.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the examples of ribbon diversity across different sensory systems presented in the preceding text

claim: The functional requirements of synaptic transmission differ not only across neuron types, but also within.
source: However, the functional requirements of synaptic transmission do not only differ across neuron types, but also within (Baden et al., 2013b; Franceschini et al., 1981; Sinha et al., 2017; Szatko et al., 2019; Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b; Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Baden et al., 2013b; Franceschini et al., 1981; Sinha et al., 2017; Szatko et al., 2019; Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b; Zimmermann et al., 2018

claim: Different parts of the eye survey different parts of visual space, often with distinct distribution of light and visuo-ecological significance.
source: For example, in vision, different parts of the eye survey different parts of visual space, often with distinct distribution of light and visuo-ecological significance (reviewed in Baden et al., 2020; Land and Nilsson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles by Baden et al., 2020 and Land and Nilsson, 2012

claim: Larval zebrafish UV-cone photoreceptors exhibit profound structural, molecular, and circuit differences depending on their location in the eye.
source: We explored this idea in the model of larval zebrafish UV-cone photoreceptors, which exhibit profound structural, molecular, and circuit differences depending on their location in the eye (Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b

claim: UV-cone density varies across retinal regions and peaks in the acute zone (AZ), and to a lesser extent also nasally.
source: First, UV-cone density varies across retinal regions and peaks in the acute zone (AZ), and to a lesser extent also nasally (Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b; Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b and Zimmermann et al., 2018

claim: UV-cones in the AZ combine an enlarged outer segment with molecular tuning of the phototransduction cascade, an elevated calcium baseline and strong feedback from horizontal cells to boost detection brighter-than-background stimuli.
source: Furthermore, UV-cones in the AZ combine an enlarged outer segment with molecular tuning of the phototransduction cascade, an elevated calcium baseline and strong feedback from horizontal cells to boost detection brighter-than-background stimuli.
evidence: This statement is part of a discussion about UV-cone properties, which is supported by citation to Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b in the preceding sentence

claim: UV-cones in the AZ support visual prey capture of UV-bright water-borne microorganisms such as paramecia.
source: This likely supports visual prey capture of UV-bright water-borne microorganisms such as paramecia.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of AZ UV-cones based on their properties

claim: UV-cones in non-AZ parts of the eye preferentially respond to darker-than-background stimuli.
source: In contrast, UV-cones in other parts of the eye preferentially respond to darker-than-background stimuli, which may serve silhouette detection of nearby objects against the backdrop of bright UV-scatter from the sun.
evidence: This statement is part of a discussion about UV-cone properties, which is supported by citation to Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b earlier in the paragraph

claim: Non-AZ UV-cones differ in additional aspects, including their absolute light sensitivity.
source: Amongst themselves, non-AZ UV-cones further differ in additional aspects, including their absolute light sensitivity.
evidence: This statement is part of a discussion about UV-cone properties, which is supported by citation to Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b earlier in the paragraph

claim: Dorsal ribbons were smaller compared to AZ or nasal ones.
source: This revealed that dorsal ribbons were smaller (Figure 1d, e) and less numerous (Figure 1f) compared to AZ or nasal ones.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and 1e

claim: Dorsal ribbons were less numerous compared to AZ or nasal ones.
source: This revealed that dorsal ribbons were smaller (Figure 1d, e) and less numerous (Figure 1f) compared to AZ or nasal ones.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f

claim: Nasal UV-cones had the lowest vesicle density immediately adjacent to the ribbon.
source: However, nasal UV-cones had the lowest vesicle density immediately adjacent to the ribbon (Figure 1g, h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g, h, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Further away from the ribbon, the vesicle density was lowest in dorsal UV-cones and highest in AZ UV-cones.
source: In addition, further away from the ribbon, the vesicle density was lowest in dorsal UV-cones and highest in AZ UV-cones (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The overall complement between ribbon number, geometry, and vesicle distributions markedly differed across the three regions of the eye.
source: Taken together, the overall complement between ribbon number, geometry, and vesicle distributions therefore markedly differed across the three regions of the eye (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Different eye regions exhibited different glutamate signals during light offsets, despite similar appearing calcium signals.
source: In example recordings from each eye region, this revealed different glutamate signals during light offsets, despite similar appearing calcium signals (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c

claim: When scaled to their common sustained component, the dorsal cone glutamate release was much more transient compared to the nasal cone glutamate release, with a kinetically intermediate AZ cone.
source: When scaled to their common sustained component, the dorsal cone glutamate release was much more transient compared to the nasal cone glutamate release, with a kinetically intermediate AZ cone (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Both at the level of calcium and glutamate, nasal UV-cones exhibited small peak amplitudes.
source: In particular, both at the level of calcium (Figure 3c) and glutamate (Figure 3d), nasal UV-cones exhibited small peak amplitudes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and 3d

claim: The glutamate release of AZ UV-cones was increased during the 50% contrast period at the start of the stimulus.
source: In addition, the glutamate release of AZ UV-cones was increased during the 50% contrast period at the start of the stimulus (Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f

claim: The AZ calcium baseline appeared elevated, but this difference was not statistically significant.
source: In line with previous work, the AZ calcium baseline also appeared elevated (Figure 3a); however, this difference was not statistically significant (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and 3e

claim: All regions exhibited notably stronger adaptation during the first flash.
source: For this, we analysed the first flash response separately from the mean of subsequent ones because all regions exhibited notably stronger adaptation during the first flash (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Dorsal UV-cones exhibited the most pronounced within-pulse adaptation.
source: Overall, this consistently revealed the most pronounced within-pulse adaptation in dorsal UV-cones (Figure 3g, h), but no significant differences in the sustained components (Figure 3i, j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g and 3h

claim: There were no significant differences in the sustained components across regions.
source: Overall, this consistently revealed the most pronounced within-pulse adaptation in dorsal UV-cones (Figure 3g, h), but no significant differences in the sustained components (Figure 3i, j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i and 3j

claim: The kinetics of calcium responses were similar to each other across the three zones.
source: The kinetics of calcium responses were similar to each other across the three zones (Figure 3k), thus broadly supporting our previous results based on jRGeco measurements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3k

claim: Rise kinetics of calcium responses were similar across all zones.
source: First, we found similar rise kinetics across all zones (Figure 3l) which therefore unlikely linked to the differences observed at the level of glutamate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l

claim: The calcium response in the AZ was weakly but significantly advanced (i.e. it occurred earlier) compared to nasally or dorsally.
source: Nevertheless, the response in the AZ was weakly but significantly advanced (i.e. it occurred earlier) compared to nasally or dorsally (Figure 3n).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3n

claim: Decay kinetics were significantly faster in AZ cones compared to dorsal cones.
source: Moreover, decay kinetics were significantly faster in AZ cones compared to dorsal cones (Figure 3m) contrary to the adaptation index of the glutamate recordings (Figure 3g, i), hinting that the release dynamics were shaped differentially by the synaptic machinery across zones.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3m

claim: The model fitted the functional data well and accurately modelled the pronounced first UV-flash response differences between zones.
source: The model fitted the functional data well and accurately modelled the pronounced first UV-flash response differences between zones (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by model predictions shown in Figure 4c

claim: The calcium offset (x0) was markedly increased in the nasal model.
source: This allowed pinpointing possible key differences: for example, the calcium offset (x0, which can be understood as the inverted calcium baseline; Materials and methods) was markedly increased in the nasal model (Figure 4d, e).
evidence: Supported by model inference results shown in Figure 4d and 4e

claim: For RRP sizes and associated maximal refill rates, the model required the smallest values nasally.
source: For RRP sizes and associated maximal refill rates, the model required the smallest values nasally (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by model inference results shown in Figure 4e

claim: The parameter posteriors were mostly uncorrelated, indicating that there is only little structure in the optimal parameter landscape.
source: Interestingly, with few exceptions (e.g. the maximal release rate and calcium offset), the parameter posteriors were mostly uncorrelated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), indicating that there is only little structure in the optimal parameter landscape.
evidence: Supported by model inference results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: The model and data leave little room for possible compensatory mechanisms as this would result in clear correlations of the involved parameters.
source: This also suggests that the model and data leave little room for possible compensatory mechanisms as this would result in a clear correlations of the involved parameters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that parameter posteriors were mostly uncorrelated

claim: The match between the model output and measured glutamate release for a calcium input was generally worse for parameters corresponding to a different region.
source: The match between the model output and measured glutamate release for a calcium input was generally worse for parameters corresponding to a different region, confirming that our release models were indeed regionally specific.
evidence: This is based on the model comparison analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 4f, g

claim: The sustained component of the AZ could not be captured by either the dorsal or nasal models.
source: For example, the sustained component of the AZ could not be captured by either the dorsal or nasal models (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4g

claim: The models produced different transient behaviours independent of the calcium inputs.
source: Moreover, the models produced different transient behaviours independent of the calcium inputs (Figure 4f, g).
evidence: Supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4f and 4g

claim: The region-specific models evaluated on self calcium inputs outperformed the models on non-self inputs.
source: The model differences were especially high on the relevant loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), which was based on the summary statistics and paid special attention to features like transiency. However, already the mean squared error (MSE) as loss function confirmed this difference: the region-specific models evaluated on self calcium inputs outperformed the models on non-self inputs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and 1c

claim: The linear model captured the general shape of the flash responses, but was not able to model glutamate transients nor adaptation over several flashes.
source: While as expected the linear model captured the general shape of the flash responses, it was not able to model glutamate transients nor adaptation over several flashes (Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4h

claim: The biophysical model outperformed the linear model in terms of the MSE.
source: The biophysical model also outperformed the linear model in terms of the MSE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: The Sobol indices revealed a generally high influence of the calcium parameters (x0 and k) during UV-bright periods and around light-dark transitions in all three zones.
source: The Sobol indices revealed a generally high influence of the calcium parameters (x0 and k) during UV-bright periods and around light-dark transitions in all three zones (Figure 5a–c, top row).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 5a-c

claim: Beyond an initial key role of the RRP size for shaping the first dark-flash response, pool sizes generally played only relatively minor roles.
source: In contrast, beyond an initial key role of the RRP size for shaping the first dark-flash response, pool sizes generally played only relatively minor roles (Figure 5, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 5

claim: The refilling rate of the IP from the RP (JRP_IP) was increasingly critical for shaping dark flash responses in the AZ model but had comparatively little influence in the nasal model.
source: For example, the refilling rate of the IP from the RP (JRP_IP) was increasingly critical for shaping dark flash responses in the AZ model (Figure 5a, blue) but had comparatively little influence in the nasal model (Figure 5b, blue).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 5a and 5b

claim: The maximal release rate (JExo) particularly influenced the variance in early dark flash responses in the dorsal model.
source: In contrast, the maximal release rate (JExo) particularly influenced the variance in early dark flash responses in the dorsal model (Figure 5c, green), while nasally refilling of the RRP from the IP (JIP_RRP) played a greater role (Figure 5b, yellow).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 5c

claim: Nasally, refilling of the RRP from the IP (JIP_RRP) played a greater role in influencing the variance in early dark flash responses.
source: In contrast, the maximal release rate (JExo) particularly influenced the variance in early dark flash responses in the dorsal model (Figure 5c, green), while nasally refilling of the RRP from the IP (JIP_RRP) played a greater role (Figure 5b, yellow).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 5b

claim: The rates of vesicle transfer between pools, rather than the pool sizes themselves or their calcium dependence, may underpin the experimentally observed region-wise differences in release properties from zebrafish UV-cones in vivo.
source: Together, this analysis suggests that particularly the rates of vesicle transfer between pools, rather than the pool sizes themselves or their calcium dependence, may underpin the experimentally observed region-wise differences in release properties from zebrafish UV-cones in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sensitivity analysis results

claim: The model reproduced the trends previously measured in vivo, including the low maximal activation nasally, the largest transient component dorsally, and the largest sustained component in the AZ.
source: As expected, this reproduced the trends previously measured in vivo, including the low maximal activation nasally (Figure 6a), the largest transient component dorsally (Figure 6b), and the largest sustained component in the AZ (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 6a-c

claim: Both maximal activation and the size of the sustained component could be tuned by varying RRP and/or IP pool sizes, with negligible contributions from the maximal release rate or the calcium offset.
source: Exploring this model (Figure 6d–f), we found that both maximal activation (Figure 6d) and the size of the sustained component (Figure 6f) could be tuned by varying RRP and/or IP pool sizes (left column), with negligible contributions from the maximal release rate or the calcium offset (right column).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 6d and 6f

claim: The transient component primarily hinged on the maximal release rate, with more complex additional contributions from the interplay of vesicle pool sizes.
source: In contrast, the transient component primarily hinged on the maximal release rate (Figure 6e, right column), with more complex additional contributions from the interplay of vesicle pool sizes (left column).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 6e

claim: Transient and sustained responses can be defined by largely non-overlapping properties of the ribbon, possibly providing a powerful handle for their independent tuning.
source: Accordingly, our generalised model suggests that transient and sustained responses can be defined by largely non-overlapping properties of the ribbon, possibly providing a powerful handle for their independent tuning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model exploration results

claim: The calcium offset (x0) is a key parameter for the detectability of a high-amplitude dark event amongst an otherwise noisy stimulus sequence.
source: This highlighted the calcium offset (x0) as a key parameter (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7b

claim: Once x0 is set, additional benefits for dark event detection could be gained from increasing RRP-size but only small benefits from increasing IP size.
source: Once x0 is set, additional benefits could be gained from increasing RRP-size but only small benefits from increasing IP size (Figure 7c), ideally in further combination with a high maximal release rate (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7c and 7d

claim: Beyond an inverse dependence on calcium baseline, the ribbon parameters that benefitted the detection of on- and off-events were virtually identical.
source: This showed that beyond an inverse dependence on calcium baseline (Figure 7f, cf. Figure 7b), the ribbon parameters that benefitted the detection of on- and off-events were in fact virtually identical (Figure 7g, h, cf. Figure 7c, d).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7f-h

claim: The low calcium offset (i.e. high baseline) supporting the detection of on-events is in line with previous work showing the AZ had highest calcium baseline and an enhanced ability to detect visuoecologically important UV-on events such as the presence of prey.
source: The low calcium offset (i.e. high baseline) supporting the detection of on-events is in line with our previous work (Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b), where the AZ showed highest calcium baseline and an enhanced ability to detect visuoecologically important UV-on events such as the presence of prey.
evidence: This connects current model results with previous experimental findings from Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b

claim: The ability to transmit fast temporal flicker primarily depended on the calcium kinetics rather than the specific tuning of the ribbon itself.
source: This revealed that this property primarily depended on the calcium kinetics rather than the specific tuning of the ribbon itself (Figure 7i–k).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7i-k

claim: Beyond calcium dynamics, the calcium offset as well as an approximate balance of medium-sized pools for both the RRP and IP could provide additional support for encoding high-frequency components.
source: Beyond calcium dynamics (here, fixing the time constant τ for calcium at 0.5 s), again the calcium offset (Figure 7j) as well as an approximate balance of medium-sized pools for both the RRP and IP (Figure 7k), could provide additional support for encoding high-frequency components.
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7j and 7k

claim: Both UV-cone ribbon ultrastructure and their effective synaptic transfer systematically differed between regions.
source: Our findings that both UV-cone ribbon ultrastructure (Figure 1) and their effective synaptic transfer (Figures 2 and 3) systematically differed between regions support the notion that these two sets of properties are linked (Regus-Leidig and Brandstätter, 2012; Sterling and Matthews, 2005; Wichmann and Moser, 2015).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1-3, with additional support from citations

claim: Building a direct bridge between ultrastructural and functional properties of ribbons remains difficult.
source: However, building a direct bridge between them remains difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in linking structure and function

claim: The size of a ribbon is expected to be linked to the number of vesicles it can hold.
source: For example, the size of a ribbon is expected to be linked to the number of vesicles it can hold.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ribbon structure-function relationships

claim: Looking at ribbon geometry alone may be insufficient to accurately predict effective pool sizes.
source: This strongly suggests that looking at ribbon geometry alone may be insufficient to accurately predict effective pool sizes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that vesicle density varies independently of ribbon size

claim: Joint consideration of ribbon area and vesicle density may be more informative for predicting effective pool sizes.
source: Instead, joint consideration of ribbon area and vesicle density may be more informative as supported by our model, which produced a near-identical IP size and generally low RRP sizes for both nasal and dorsal UV-cones (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is an inference supported by model results shown in Figure 4e

claim: AZ cones combined large ribbons with a high vesicle density near the ribbon, and the model predicted the largest RRP size for them.
source: In agreement, AZ cones combined large ribbons with a high vesicle density near the ribbon, and in their case the model did predict the largest RRP size (though a similar IP size).
evidence: This connects structural observations with model predictions

claim: Model IP sizes generally stayed near the prior and exhibited low Sobol indices, suggesting that this property was not critical for explaining the glutamate responses to the test stimulus.
source: Notably, model IP sizes generally stayed near the prior (Figure 4e) and exhibited low Sobol indices (Figure 5), which suggests that this property was not critical for explaining the glutamate responses to our relatively slow and simple test stimulus which was necessitated by the generally low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) of jRGeco1b signals (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from model results shown in Figures 4e and 5

claim: Regionally distinct IP-size estimates might emerge when fitted to responses to different stimuli.
source: It remains possible that regionally distinct IP-size estimates would emerge in response when fitted to responses to different stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future findings

claim: An elevated vesicle density further away from the ribbon in AZ UV-cones is potentially indicative of an increased RP and/or an increased rate of IP refilling.
source: Beyond ribbon sizes, our ultrastructural analysis further highlighted an elevated vesicle density further away from the ribbon in AZ UV-cones (Figure 1g, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), potentially indicative of an increased RP and/or an increased rate of IP refilling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural data shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The model produced only minor differences in IP refill rates between regions, but in the reversed order compared to what might be expected from vesicle density.
source: However, the model produced only minor differences in IP refill rates between regions, but in the reversed order (Figure 4e), and for simplicity RP size was fixed because it did not strongly affect function within the tens of seconds timescales interrogated (Baden et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Figure 4e, with additional support from citation to Baden et al., 2014

claim: A direct link between UV-cone RP vesicle density and function remains outstanding.
source: Accordingly, a direct link between UV-cone RP vesicle density and function remains outstanding.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge

claim: The elevated RP vesicle density in AZ cones could be helpful for supporting the particularly high total vesicle turnover at longer timescales.
source: Conceivably, this property could be helpful for supporting the particularly high total vesicle turnover in AZ cones (Figure 3d, f, i) at longer timescales.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting structural observations with functional data shown in Figure 3d, f, i

claim: Dorsal cones' release was particularly transient, as would be suited for pulsatile, rather than continuous transmission.
source: At the level of measured function, dorsal cones stood out in that their release was particularly transient (Figure 3a, g, h) as would be suited for pulsatile, rather than continuous transmission.
evidence: This connects functional data shown in Figure 3a, g, h with an interpretation about transmission mode

claim: Dorsal cones' generally small but densely populated ribbons and small RP may be well suited to support pulsatile transmission.
source: Their generally small but densely populated ribbons and small RP may be well suited to support this property.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking structural properties to functional properties

claim: The model predicted a faster RRP refill rate in dorsal cones, which might be useful to ensure the RRP is rapidly replenished after each pulse.
source: In possible agreement, the model predicted a faster RRP refill rate in dorsal cones, which might be useful to ensure the RRP is rapidly replenished after each pulse.
evidence: This connects model predictions with a functional interpretation

claim: The effective absence of any transient component in nasal UV-cones resulted in the model predicting the lowest RRP refill rate.
source: Conversely, the effective absence of any transient component nasal UV-cones (Figure 3a, g, h) in the model resulted in the lowest RRP refill rate, which may appear counterintuitive, but paired with a small nasal RRP resulted in the sustained response behaviour observed in Figure 4f.
evidence: This connects functional data shown in Figure 3a, g, h with model predictions and results shown in Figure 4f

claim: The low RRP refill rate in nasal cones may further link to the low IP occupancy in nasal UV-cones observed under EM.
source: Additionally, this may further link to the abovementioned low IP occupancy in nasal UV-cones, as observed under EM (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is an inference connecting model predictions with structural data shown in Figure 1g

claim: The nasal model simultaneously predicted the smallest RRP but the largest RRP release rate, resulting in a situation where the very few vesicles ready for release were immediately dumped.
source: Moreover, the nasal model simultaneously predicted the smallest RRP but the largest RRP release rate, which resulted in a situation where the very few vesicles ready for release were immediately dumped, thus preventing the build-up of vesicles that enable the transients of dorsal and AZ UV-cones.
evidence: This is an interpretation of model predictions

claim: Most functional differences across retinal regions appeared at the level of glutamate, whereas only subtle differences in the dynamics were observed at the level of calcium.
source: Importantly, most functional differences across retinal regions appeared at the level of glutamate, whereas only subtle differences in the dynamics were observed at the level of calcium.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented earlier

claim: The faster decay in AZ is linked to horizontal cells as reported previously.
source: The faster decay in AZ (Figure 3m) is linked to horizontal cells as reported previously (Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b), and the temporally advanced calcium signals measured in the AZ by GCaMP6f (Figure 3n) cannot explain the differences in the glutamate dynamics.
evidence: This connects current findings shown in Figure 3m with previous work from Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b

claim: The temporally advanced calcium signals measured in the AZ by GCaMP6f cannot explain the differences in the glutamate dynamics.
source: The faster decay in AZ (Figure 3m) is linked to horizontal cells as reported previously (Yoshimatsu et al., 2020b), and the temporally advanced calcium signals measured in the AZ by GCaMP6f (Figure 3n) cannot explain the differences in the glutamate dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 3n

claim: While it remains possible that the iGluSnFR recordings slightly distorted the time courses of glutamate signals, it is unlikely to strongly affect the conclusions because any such effects would apply equally to all measured eye regions.
source: Moreover, while it remains possible that the iGluSnFR recordings slightly distorted the time courses of glutamate signals, it is unlikely to strongly affect our conclusions because any such effects would apply equally to all measured eye regions.
evidence: This is a statement about potential limitations and their impact on conclusions

claim: It remains difficult to make definitive links between ribbon structure and function.
source: Taken together, while it remains difficult to make definitive links between ribbon structure and function, a number of inferences can be drawn which may usefully inform our understanding of the ribbon's role in moulding synaptic transmission to specific needs.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the challenges in linking structure and function

claim: It will be interesting to explore to what extent the differential ribbon tunings described for larvae are also a characteristic of UV-cones in adult zebrafish.
source: In the future it will be interesting to explore to what extent the differential ribbon tunings described here for larvae are also a characteristic of UV-cones in adult zebrafish.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions

claim: Adults feature a crystalline cone mosaic, meaning that numerical anisotropies in cones as they occur in larvae are not expected.
source: Adults feature a crystalline cone mosaic (reviewed in Baden, 2021), meaning that numerical anisotropies in cones as they occur in larvae (Zimmermann et al., 2018) are not expected.
evidence: Supported by citations to Baden, 2021 and Zimmermann et al., 2018

claim: The absence of numerical anisotropies in adult zebrafish does not preclude the possibility that UV-cones have different properties across the retina.
source: However, this does not preclude the possibility that UV-cones have different properties across the retina.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what the structural differences do and do not imply

claim: Adult zebrafish display a much broader array of visual behaviours compared to larvae.
source: While adult zebrafish display a much broader array of visual behaviours compared to larvae, their visual ecology remains poorly explored, which makes it difficult to predict what UV-cone tunings – if any – might be expected.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about zebrafish behavior

claim: The visual ecology of adult zebrafish remains poorly explored.
source: While adult zebrafish display a much broader array of visual behaviours compared to larvae, their visual ecology remains poorly explored, which makes it difficult to predict what UV-cone tunings – if any – might be expected.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge

claim: The presented model is a modified version of the basic framework used in Baden et al., 2014.
source: The presented model (Figure 4a) is a modified version of the basic framework used in Baden et al., 2014.

claim: The approach was extended by combining simulation-based inference with simultaneous calcium and glutamate recordings to extensively expand the analysis of the model.

claim: The continuous model enabled the use of available software toolboxes.

claim: With the simulation-based inference approach, full posterior distributions were obtained rather than point estimates.
source: With the simulation-based inference approach (Figure 4b) we obtained full posterior distributions (Figure 4e) rather than point estimates which can lead to overconfident or incorrect conclusions in the case of an under-constrained model or 'sloppy' model parameters.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the inference approach

claim: Posterior estimates can be seen as a global method to identify sloppy and stiff parameters.
source: At the same time, posterior estimates can be seen as a global method to identify sloppy and stiff parameters (in contrast to local methods as in Gutenkunst et al., 2007) and additionally allowed us to conduct a sensitivity analysis by computing the first Sobol indices (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the inference approach, with citation to Gutenkunst et al., 2007

claim: The Sobol indices showed zone-dependent, biologically interpretable time courses.
source: These focus on the variance of the model output rather than on the variance of the posterior distributions and showed zone-dependent, biologically interpretable time courses.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of the sensitivity analysis

claim: A simple step stimulus is sufficient to show the influence of different anatomical properties on features of the signal.
source: This highlighted a time-varying dependence of the release on the model parameters. It indicates that already a simple step stimulus is sufficient to show the influence of different anatomical properties on features of the signal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sensitivity analysis results

claim: For all investigated properties, the baseline and dynamics of the calcium signal were critical.
source: For all investigated properties, we observed that the baseline and dynamics of the calcium signal were critical (Figure 7b, f, i), whereupon the anatomical ribbon properties allowed fine-tuning the final output behaviour (Figure 7c, g, k).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7b, f, i

claim: The anatomical ribbon properties allowed fine-tuning the final output behaviour.
source: For all investigated properties, we observed that the baseline and dynamics of the calcium signal were critical (Figure 7b, f, i), whereupon the anatomical ribbon properties allowed fine-tuning the final output behaviour (Figure 7c, g, k).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7c, g, k

claim: The influence of the calcium baseline for the detection of high-frequency events followed a bimodal distribution with intermediate values offering the poorest performance.
source: Interestingly, the influence of the calcium baseline for the detection of high-frequency events followed a bimodal distribution (Figure 7j) with intermediate values offering the poorest performance.
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7j

claim: The calcium baseline may present a key variable that enables ribbons to trade-off the transmission of high-frequency stimuli against providing an approximately balanced on- and off-response behaviour.
source: In combination with the approximately equal and opposite effects of calcium baseline on the detectability of on- and off-events (Figure 7b, f), this suggests that the calcium baseline may present a key variable that enables ribbons to trade-off the transmission of high-frequency stimuli against providing an approximately balanced on- and off-response behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from model exploration results shown in Figure 7b, f, j

claim: The transmission of high-frequency events benefits from the use of a highly non-linear synapse that is either balanced to on- or off-events, but not both.
source: Vice versa, it also suggests that the transmission of high-frequency events benefits from the use of a highly non-linear synapse that is either balanced to on- or off-events, but not both.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model exploration results

claim: The bimodal dependence of release performance on resting calcium levels is likely linked to biasing the system to preferentially either increase or decrease in light, but not both, thereby thresholding out responses of the respectively opposite polarity.
source: This bimodal dependence of release performance on resting calcium levels is likely linked to biasing the system to preferentially either increase or decrease in light, but not both, thereby thresholding out responses of the respectively opposite polarity.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the bimodal distribution

claim: The time course of calcium decay was pivotal for defining the possible working range of high-frequency transmission regardless of the properties of the ribbon itself.
source: Finally, and perhaps unsurprisingly, the time course of calcium decay was pivotal for defining the possible working range of high-frequency transmission regardless of the properties of the ribbon itself (Figure 7i, cf. Figure 7j, k).
evidence: Supported by model exploration results shown in Figure 7i-k

claim: The effect of calcium decay on high-frequency transmission was especially strong for a fast calcium decay (<100 ms) which is generally associated with nanodomains.
source: This effect was especially strong for a fast calcium decay (<100 ms) which is generally associated with nanodomains (Jarsky et al., 2010) rather than decay dynamics >>100 ms for microdomains (Beaumont et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jarsky et al., 2010 and Beaumont et al., 2005

claim: To what extent nano- or microdomain signalling dominates in larval zebrafish UV-cones remains untested.
source: To what extent nano- or microdomain signalling dominates in larval zebrafish UV-cones remains untested.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge

claim: It seems likely that in larval zebrafish UV-cones, already low micromolar calcium concentrations that are typically associated with microdomains can evoke substantial release.
source: However, in view of their similarity in pedicle architecture to mammalian rods (e.g. small, single invagination site), it seems likely that also here already low micromolar calcium concentrations that are typically associated with microdomains can evoke substantial release (Thoreson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity to mammalian rods, with support from citation to Thoreson et al., 2004

claim: A primary determinant for tuning a ribbon's high-frequency response is the local stimulus-driven calcium environment around the ribbon, rather than properties of the ribbon itself.
source: In any case, a primary determinant for tuning a ribbon's high-frequency response is the local stimulus-driven calcium environment around the ribbon, rather than properties of the ribbon itself (see also Baden et al., 2014; Baden et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations to Baden et al., 2014 and Baden et al., 2013a

claim: Once the calcium environment is set, large pool sizes paired with a high release rate were generally preferable for all explored forms of signal detection.
source: Nevertheless, once this is set, large pool sizes paired with a high release rate were generally preferable for all explored forms of signal detection.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the model exploration results

claim: While the presynaptic calcium is a critical variable, even with a fixed calcium model the ribbon can be shifted into different response behaviours.
source: Taken together, our model therefore suggests that while the presynaptic calcium is a critical variable, even with a fixed calcium model the ribbon can be shifted into different response behaviours.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the model exploration results

source: The effect and importance of calcium handling have also been shown in ribbon synapses of inner hair cells, where even within an individual synaptic compartment a local variation in calcium channels can lead to different transfer functions at different release sides (Özçete and Moser, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Özçete and Moser, 2021
